H1.text: Liquid oxygen sticks to a magnet. Liquid nitrogen runs straight past it. And two helium atoms never stay together.

H2.text: Three puzzles. The bond picture we know so far cannot explain the first one.

H3.text: Aarav hears a clue in the school corridor. Two phones play the same tone.

H4.text: In some spots the sound adds up and gets louder. In other spots it cancels and almost disappears.

H5.text: Electron waves do the same inside molecules. By the end, you will know which molecules can exist, and which are magnetic.

P1.text: So what is new in this theory?

P2.text: In valence bond theory, each electron still belongs to its own atom's orbital.

P3.text: In molecular orbital theory, the atomic orbitals merge. The electrons now belong to the whole molecule. Hund and Mulliken built this idea in 1932.

P4.text: The new orbitals are called molecular orbitals. We make them by adding or subtracting the atomic orbitals.

P5.text: This is called L C A O, the linear combination of atomic orbitals. Combination means adding or subtracting.

P6.text: Two atomic orbitals go in, two molecular orbitals come out. Count in equals count out.

S1.text: Let's watch two hydrogen atoms on our molecule bench.

S2.text: When the two waves add up, like the loud spots, electron cloud builds up between the nuclei. Both nuclei pull on it.

S3.text: This is a bonding molecular orbital, sigma one s. Its energy is lower than the atomic orbitals.

S4.text: When the waves cancel, like the quiet spots, there is an empty gap between the nuclei. This gap is called a node.

S5.text: This is an antibonding orbital, sigma star one s. Its energy is higher.

S6.text: Now fill in the electrons. Lowest energy first, two per orbital, with opposite spins.

S7.text: Hydrogen's two electrons both go into the bonding orbital. The molecule is lower in energy than two lone atoms. So H two is stable.

B1.text: Now helium. Each helium atom brings two electrons, so four in total.

B2.text: Two fill the bonding orbital. The other two must go into the antibonding orbital.

B3.text: The antibonding pair undoes the work of the bonding pair.

B4.text: Pause and think. Can two helium atoms form a stable molecule?

B5.text: No! The gain and the loss cancel out. That is why He two does not exist.

D1.text: Let's turn this into a number, one link at a time.

D2.text: Link one. N b is the number of electrons in bonding orbitals.

D3.text: Link two. N a is the number of electrons in antibonding orbitals.

D4.text: Link three. Bond order is half of N b minus N a.

D5.text: Link four. Bond order zero means no molecule. A positive bond order means a stable molecule.

D6.text: Link five. A higher bond order means a shorter and stronger bond.

T1.text: Remember this. Bonding electrons hold atoms together. Antibonding electrons pull them apart.

W1.text: Now, one worked example. Why does oxygen stick to a magnet?

W2.text: Step one. Two oxygen atoms bring sixteen electrons. Fill them in order, lowest energy first.

W3.text: Step two. Ten electrons sit in bonding orbitals, and six sit in antibonding orbitals.

W4.text: Step three. Bond order is half of ten minus six. That is two, a double bond.

W5.text: Step four. The last two electrons go into two equal pi star orbitals. By Hund's rule, they sit one in each, with the same spin.

W6.text: Two unpaired electrons make oxygen paramagnetic. That means a magnet pulls it in. Valence bond theory could not explain this.

C1.text: Now compare four molecules side by side.

C2.text: Hydrogen, bond order one. All its electrons are paired, so it is diamagnetic. A magnet pushes it away, very weakly.

C3.text: Helium, bond order zero. It does not exist.

C4.text: Nitrogen, bond order three. All paired, so diamagnetic. That is why liquid nitrogen runs past the magnet.

C5.text: Oxygen, bond order two. Two unpaired electrons, so paramagnetic.

C6.text: One more detail. Up to nitrogen, the pi two p orbitals fill before sigma two p. From oxygen on, sigma two p fills first.

X2.text: Oxygen has sixteen electrons, an even number. So students say all of them are paired, and call oxygen diamagnetic.

X3.text: Wrong. An even count can still leave lone electrons. Oxygen's last two sit alone in two pi star orbitals. So oxygen is paramagnetic.

E1.text: Where is this asked? Both JEE Main and NEET. Bond order and magnetic behaviour of molecules and ions.

Q1.text: Exam level now. Which of these has the highest bond order? Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is B. O two plus.

A2.text: Oxygen has bond order two, with two electrons in the pi star orbitals.

A3.text: O two plus loses one of those antibonding electrons. N b is ten, N a is five. Half of five is two point five.

A4.text: Adding electrons does the opposite. O two minus has one point five, and O two two minus has one. C traps students who think more electrons make a stronger bond.

Y3.text: Two. Why does He two not exist?
